blocks.title: Arrays and positions

outcomes.foundation: Read an array safely and find the first matching position.
outcomes.interview: Trace a single-pass array scan without an off-by-one error.
outcomes.professional_transfer: Choose an indexed representation when direct position lookup is more valuable than cheap middle insertion.

blocks.target: Read an array safely and find the first matching position.
blocks.expected_complexity: Index lookup is O(1); a complete scan is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

selection_dimensions: the input has stable positions
direct lookup by position matters
middle insertion is not the dominant operation

blocks.theory: An array stores items at numbered positions, starting at zero. In [7, 2, 9, 4], position 2 holds 9. For n items, read only positions 0 through n - 1. A scan checks each position once and stops when it reaches n. Direct indexing takes O(1), while a complete scan takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Inserting in the middle can take O(n) because later items must move.

visual.label: Array of length 4; i is the next position to inspect.
visual.prediction_checkpoint: Before revealing state 3, predict whether i may advance again and name the bounds condition.

states.message: i = 0 is valid; inspect 7.
i = 3 is valid; inspect 4.
Stop before reading: i = n is outside the array.

blocks.title: Hash tables and collisions

outcomes.foundation: Store and find values by key, including when keys share a bucket.
outcomes.interview: Use a lookup table while qualifying expected versus worst-case cost.
outcomes.professional_transfer: Choose a key-based index when lookup by identity is central and collision/load behavior is acceptable.

blocks.target: Store and find values by key, including when keys share a bucket.
blocks.expected_complexity: Lookup and insertion are expected O(1) with a controlled load factor; collision chains can make a lookup O(n) in the worst case. Auxiliary space is O(k) for k stored keys.

selection_dimensions: lookup is by key identity
expected cost is acceptable under stated hashing assumptions
ordered traversal is not the primary need

blocks.theory: A hash table stores a value under a key. A hash function chooses a bucket, but different keys can choose the same bucket: this is a collision. If 'ant' and 'bee' share a bucket, lookup must compare the stored keys to find the right value. Keeping colliding entries together is called chaining. Lookup is expected O(1) when hashes spread keys well and the table grows with its contents; a bucket containing every key takes O(n) to search.

visual.label: Three buckets; collisions are stored as a chain and resolved with key equality.
visual.prediction_checkpoint: Before revealing state 3, predict what the lookup must compare after it reaches bucket 1.

states.message: hash('ant') selects bucket 1.
'bee' collides with 'ant'; both entries remain reachable.
Compare keys in bucket 1 until 'bee' matches.

blocks.title: Two pointers in a sorted array

outcomes.foundation: Find a pair by safely discarding one end at a time.
outcomes.interview: Trace a sorted-pair search with a one-way movement argument.
outcomes.professional_transfer: Recognize when ordered data and a monotone condition permit one-pass boundary narrowing.

blocks.target: Find a pair by safely discarding one end at a time.
blocks.expected_complexity: Each pointer moves in one direction at most n times, so the trace is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

prerequisites: Hash-table lookup and collision reasoning (contrast only)
selection_dimensions: the data is ordered or can be ordered
a comparison yields a safe monotone move
linear extra space is undesirable or ordering is otherwise useful

blocks.theory: Place one pointer at each end of a sorted array. To find a target pair sum, add the two values. If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right: using that same left value with any smaller right value would also be too small. If the sum is too large, move the right pointer left for the same reason in reverse. Stop at a match or when the pointers meet. Each pointer moves in one direction, so the scan takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

visual.label: Sorted values [1, 3, 4, 8, 11], target 15; left and right bound viable pairs.
visual.prediction_checkpoint: Before revealing state 3, predict which pointer moves after 3 + 11 and state which pairs are discarded.

states.message: 1 + 11 = 12, which is too small; move left rightward.
3 + 11 = 14, which is still too small; move left rightward again.
4 + 11 = 15; the target pair is found.

blocks.title: Binary search

outcomes.foundation: Find a value by halving the remaining sorted interval.
outcomes.interview: Explain why each comparison discards half the remaining candidates.
outcomes.professional_transfer: Choose indexed logarithmic lookup when ordered data justifies update costs.

blocks.target: Find a value by halving the remaining sorted interval.
blocks.expected_complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) extra space.

selection_dimensions: input is sorted
random indexing is available
a monotone comparison can eliminate an interval

blocks.theory: Binary search finds a value in sorted data by repeatedly checking the middle. Here both endpoints are included. If the middle value is smaller than the target, discard it and everything to its left. If it is larger, discard it and everything to its right. Any possible match stays between the endpoints. Stop when a match is found or left becomes greater than right. Each comparison halves the remaining interval, giving O(log n) time and O(1) extra space.

visual.label: Sorted values [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 21], target 16; brackets are the candidate interval.
visual.prediction_checkpoint: Before state 3, predict the new left boundary after 12 is too small.

states.message: middle 8 is too small; candidates 0 through 2 are discarded.
middle 16 matches; the interval still stated where a target could be.
For target 12, the matching singleton interval gives the answer.

blocks.title: Changing linked-list connections

outcomes.foundation: Insert or remove a node while keeping the remaining list connected.
outcomes.interview: Trace insertion or removal without losing the remaining suffix.
outcomes.professional_transfer: Choose node links when local rewiring matters more than indexed access.

blocks.target: Insert or remove a node while keeping the remaining list connected.
blocks.expected_complexity: Traversal is O(n); insertion or removal after a known predecessor is O(1) time and O(1) extra space.

selection_dimensions: local insertion or removal follows a known node
indexed lookup is not central
a head-to-tail connection contract is explicit

blocks.theory: A linked list stores a next-node reference at each node. In A → B → C, removing B means changing A.next to C. Reading B.next before changing links keeps the remaining list available. Inserting X between A and B needs two steps: first set X.next to B, then set A.next to X. Each local change takes O(1) when the previous node is already known; finding that node can take O(n).

blocks.title: Stacks and queues

outcomes.foundation: Choose which item should leave next: the newest or the oldest.
outcomes.interview: Select a stack or queue and justify processing order.
outcomes.professional_transfer: Choose an explicit collection policy for undo, scheduling, or breadth-oriented processing.

blocks.target: Choose which item should leave next: the newest or the oldest.
blocks.expected_complexity: Push/enqueue and pop/dequeue are O(1) with an appropriate representation; storage is O(n).

selection_dimensions: processing order is the main decision
items are added and removed incrementally
front/back or top state can be represented explicitly

blocks.theory: A stack removes the newest item first; a queue removes the oldest. After adding A, B, C, a stack returns C and a queue returns A. Use a stack for undo history or unfinished nested work. Use a queue for jobs that should run in arrival order. Check whether the structure is empty before removing an item. Use a suitable implementation: removing the front of a Python list shifts other items, whereas a deque supports efficient removal at either end.

visual.label: Items A, B, C enter; stack and queue expose different next items.
visual.prediction_checkpoint: Before state 3, predict which item each policy removes next.

states.message: B is stack top; A is queue front.

LIFO removes C; FIFO removes A.

blocks.title: Recursion on trees

outcomes.foundation: Combine child answers to compute an answer for the whole tree.
outcomes.interview: Trace a recursive tree computation with a correctness argument.
outcomes.professional_transfer: Use recursive decomposition when a hierarchy has the same contract at each child.

blocks.target: Combine child answers to compute an answer for the whole tree.
blocks.expected_complexity: A full traversal is O(n) time and O(h) call-stack space for height h.

selection_dimensions: input has parent-child hierarchy
each subtree supports the same subproblem
a base case is explicit

blocks.theory: A recursive tree function answers the same question for each subtree. To sum a tree, an absent node contributes zero. Otherwise, add the current value to the sums returned by the left and right children. If a root 4 has leaves 2 and 7, the leaves return 2 and 7 and the root returns 13. Every node is visited once, giving O(n) time. The active calls follow a path of height h, using O(h) extra space.

visual.label: Tree with root 4 and children 2 and 7; compute subtree sum.
visual.prediction_checkpoint: Before state 3, predict the value returned to the root from its right child.

states.message: Leaf 2 returns its own value because both child sums are zero.
Leaf 7 returns 7 under the same contract.
Root combines 4 + 2 + 7 and returns 13.

blocks.title: Breadth-first and depth-first search

outcomes.foundation: Visit graph vertices once and choose an order that fits the question.
outcomes.interview: Select BFS or DFS and state the visit invariant.
outcomes.professional_transfer: Choose traversal order according to nearest-layer, exhaustive exploration, or resource constraints.

blocks.target: Visit graph vertices once and choose an order that fits the question.
blocks.expected_complexity: With adjacency lists, traversal is O(V + E) time and O(V) space.

selection_dimensions: input is a graph or relation network
revisits are possible
processing order changes the useful result

blocks.theory: BFS uses a queue to visit vertices in increasing number of edges from the start. DFS uses a stack or recursive calls to follow one branch before returning. Keep a visited set so cycles do not cause repeated work. For BFS, mark each new vertex before adding it to the queue. With A connected to B and C, both are one edge away; a new neighbor of B is at most two edges away. BFS finds shortest edge counts in unweighted graphs. Both traversals take O(V + E) with adjacency lists.

visual.label: Edges A-B, A-C, B-D; BFS begins at A.
visual.prediction_checkpoint: Before state 3, predict which frontier vertex is processed next and why.

states.message: A is discovered and awaits processing.
Processing A discovers B and C; queue order preserves B before C.
Processing B discovers D once; B is not rediscovered through an existing edge.

blocks.title: Building a dynamic-programming table

outcomes.foundation: Define each table entry and build it from earlier answers.
outcomes.interview: Build and justify a small DP recurrence.
outcomes.professional_transfer: Choose cached subproblems when repeated overlapping computation dominates a direct recursion.

blocks.target: Define each table entry and build it from earlier answers.
blocks.expected_complexity: For n linear states with constant work each, O(n) time and O(n) space; some recurrences permit O(1) retained space.

selection_dimensions: subproblems overlap
a recurrence has smaller acyclic dependencies
an objective or count can be summarized in a state

blocks.theory: Dynamic programming saves answers to smaller problems and reuses them. Let ways[i] count sequences of one-step and two-step moves reaching position i. The final move came from i - 1 or i - 2, so add those two counts. Start with ways[0] = 1 for the empty sequence and ways[1] = 1. Then ways[2] = 2 and ways[3] = 3. Fill smaller positions first so every value you need is ready. This takes O(n) time; keeping only the last two values uses O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: If ways(2)=2 and ways(1)=1, what is ways(3)?
When is plain recursion acceptable?
questions.feedback: When subproblems do not overlap materially or the input is intentionally tiny.

questions.prompt: What makes a recurrence invalid?
questions.feedback: Dependencies that are undefined, cyclic without a resolution rule, or do not match the stated state meaning.

worked_example.input: Number of ways to reach 3 using steps of one or two
worked_example.model: Set ways(0)=1, ways(1)=1, ways(2)=2, then ways(3)=3. Each state depends only on completed smaller states.
worked_example.boundary_test: For n=0, return the declared base value rather than accessing negative indices.

faded_scaffold.expected_focus: Use ways[i - 1] + ways[i - 2] and state why both are ready.

independent_practice.exercise: Define a state and fill a table for the minimum number of one-or-two steps to reach 4.
independent_practice.stop_rule: Trace your answer, test the smallest input and one ordinary input, then explain its cost.
independent_practice.evidence: Your steps, expected answers, and time and memory estimates.
